# Split Report (auto-generated by src/make_split.py)

## Protocol
- Per-user chronological split. Test = each user's latest 20% ratings (at least 1); the rest is **train_full**.
- Inside train_full, the latest 20% of each user's ratings form the **validation** set; the rest is **train_core**.
- Tuning/model selection: fit on train_core, score on val. Final model: refit on train_full; evaluate on test **once** (Stage 10).
- Relevance for ranking metrics: rating >= 4.0. Models may only use columns ['user_id', 'movie_id', 'rating', 'timestamp']; is_original, genre, language, year are not model inputs.

|---|---|---|

- Test ratings per user: min 3, median 3, max 5
- Train_full matrix: 309 users x 126 movies, density 10.3%; movies with < 5 train ratings: 0
- Test time range 2024-08-15 to 2025-12-31; share of test ratings in is_original rows 13.4% (dataset 9.5%)

## Leakage checks (all asserted)
- No (user, movie) pair appears in two sets: PASS
- For every user, all training ratings are not later than that user's test ratings: PASS (same for train_core vs val)
- Index mappings, user means, item means and similarities are fitted on training data only.
- Limitation: the split is per user, so other users' later ratings can sit in training. This is the standard leave-latest-out protocol, but not a strict global-time replay.

### Cold-start policy (applies to every model and to the API)
1. Rating prediction, unseen user: movie mean (global mean if the movie is also unseen). Unseen movie, known user: user mean. Both unseen: global mean.
2. Ranking for an unseen user: popularity list re-ranked for genre/language diversity (Stage 11 fallback).
3. Unseen movies are never recommended (no model score); report their count.
4. Evaluation reports metrics on ALL test rows (with fallbacks) and on warm rows only, so the fallback does not hide model quality.

## Why a random split would be misleading (illustration on train_full only; test labels untouched)
| Hold-out of train_full | Hold-out rows | Cold-movie rows | Global-mean RMSE | Bias-baseline RMSE |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Random 20% | 832 | 0.00% | 0.840 | 0.724 |
| Latest 20% per user | 816 | 0.00% | 0.836 | 0.693 |

- A random split lets the model train on a user's later ratings and then "predict" their earlier ones: it answers a question nobody asks in production. The chronological split mimics real use: learn from the past, recommend for the future.
- Honest note: the two hold-outs give similar numbers (the chronological one is even slightly lower) because the synthetic generator has no taste drift over time and every movie has 10+ ratings. This table therefore cannot show a leakage penalty; the case for the chronological split rests on the protocol, and real data with changing tastes and new releases would behave differently.
- Cold start: no unseen users or movies occur in this split (every user has 15+ ratings, every movie 10+), so the policy above is exercised only by the API (new users) and by the unit tests, not by the evaluation.
- Caveat: 13.4% of test rows come from the provided original file (dataset: 9.5%) because their dates are scattered over the full two years while each synthetic user has ratings in a shorter window, so original rows land at the start or end of a timeline more often than in the middle (checked: 39% earliest 20%, 32% middle 60%, 29% latest 20%). They have no taste signal, so test RMSE will be slightly pessimistic; Stage 10 reports metrics with and without is_original rows.
